evidence.label: Harmonic heights and the Artin K(pi,1) conjecture
An Artin group with no geometric CAT(0) action

headline: Proves the Artin K(π,1) conjecture in finite rank, and finds an Artin group with no geometric CAT(0) action.
scope: Artin groups with finitely many standard generators. Three companion papers; the main theorems have Lean formalizations, but later corollaries in the manuscripts are not included.
plain: Artin groups are built from generators and braid-like rules, like the groups that describe tangled strings. A decades-old conjecture says a standard space built from these rules has no hidden higher holes. The first paper proves this for every Artin group with finitely many generators, with a Lean formalization listed. Two companion papers find an Artin group with no nice curved geometry and show that its special subgroups intersect well.
doesNot: This does not cover Artin groups with infinitely many generators, and the Lean note leaves out the later corollaries in the manuscripts.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Pierre Deligne, who proved the spherical case using finite real reflection arrangements
scorecard.significanceWhy: The K(π,1) conjecture is a central open problem for Artin groups, and CAT(0) actions were widely expected.

explanation:
Take two generators, a and b, with one rule: aba = bab. This is the braid group on three strands. Swap strands 1 and 2, then 2 and 3, then 1 and 2 again. You get the same braid as swapping 2 and 3, then 1 and 2, then 2 and 3. An Artin group allows such a rule for each pair of generators. A label m says both alternating words of length m are equal; the label ∞ imposes no rule[1]. Adding the rule that each generator squared is 1 gives the Coxeter group[1]. For a and b with label 3, the Coxeter group has 6 elements, like the symmetries of a triangle.

The Salvetti complex is a space with one cell of dimension |T| for each spherical subset T[2]. A subset is spherical when its Coxeter group is finite. For the braid example, the subsets ∅, {a}, {b} and {a, b} are all spherical. So the space has 1 point, 2 loops and 1 disc. Its Euler characteristic is 1 − 2 + 1 = 0. With label ∞ instead, {a, b} is not spherical. The space is two loops at a point, with Euler characteristic 1 − 2 = −1. The K(π,1) conjecture asks that this space be aspherical. That means its universal cover can shrink to a point, so all higher homotopy groups vanish.

Deligne proved the spherical case in 1972[3]. Later work covered FC type, dimension at most two, affine types and dimension at most three[4]. The general case stayed open. The first paper proves it for every Coxeter matrix on a finite set[5]. Labels may be finite or infinite, and diagrams may be disconnected[5].

The second paper asks about geometry. A CAT(0) space is one whose triangles are at least as thin as flat ones. A geometric action is proper and cocompact on such a space. Haettel recorded the expectation that every finite-rank Artin group has one[6]. Brady and Crisp showed an obstruction in two dimensions can vanish in three[7]. So a counterexample must work in every dimension. The paper proves there is an Artin group on 116 generators, with labels in {2, 3, ∞}, that has no geometric action[8].

The third paper studies parabolic subgroups, which are conjugates of subgroups generated by some of the generators[9]. It proves that the intersection of any two parabolic subgroups is parabolic[10]. A corollary is that arbitrary intersections are parabolic, and every subset has a smallest parabolic subgroup containing it[11]. The paper also claims a decidable word problem for every finite-rank Artin group[12].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has formal proofs of the contractible Salvetti cover, the 116-generator counterexample, and the parabolic intersection results. The Lean note leaves out later corollaries in the manuscripts. No specialist review of these papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds, and the three main theorems have Lean formalizations. Later corollaries are not in the Lean note. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A group with generators and, for some pairs, a rule that two alternating words of a given length are equal.
The group obtained from an Artin group by adding the rule that each generator squared is the identity.
A set of generators whose Coxeter group is finite.
A space built from cells, one for each spherical subset, whose loops form the Artin group.
Having a universal cover that can be shrunk to a point, so there are no higher-dimensional holes.
A space whose geodesic triangles are at least as thin as triangles in a flat plane.
A proper, cocompact action by isometries on a nonempty proper CAT(0) space.
A conjugate of a subgroup generated by some of the standard generators.
